topic: Ann Graybiel & Squire Lab (1999-2008): Dorsal Striatum Task-Bracketing & Amnesic Habit Loops (Patient E.P.)
visual_mode_reason: Understanding why Patient E.P. walked to the kitchen without hippocampal recall requires showing the dissociation between lesioned medial temporal hippocampus and intact dorsal striatum task-bracketing bursts.

primary_case.title: Patient E.P. (Eugene Pauly) amnesic habit retention & MIT dorsal striatum task-bracketing studies
primary_case.place: UC San Diego Memory Laboratory (Larry Squire) & MIT McGovern Institute (Ann Graybiel)

people.name: Eugene Pauly (Patient E.P.)
people.role: Retired aerospace technician who lost medial temporal lobes to 1992 viral encephalitis yet retained and acquired daily motor habits

people.name: Larry R. Squire
people.role: UC San Diego neuroscientist who documented E.P.'s intact habit learning despite zero declarative recall

people.name: Ann M. Graybiel
people.role: MIT neurobiologist who discovered start-and-end task-bracketing ensembles in the dorsal striatum

people.name: Kyle S. Smith
people.role: Neuroscientist who demonstrated optogenetic switching of striatal habit loops

core_facts.fact: In 1992, herpes simplex encephalitis destroyed Patient Eugene Pauly's bilateral medial temporal lobes, studied extensively by Larry Squire's team through 1999 and beyond.
Eugene could not draw a floor plan of his own house or point toward the street from his living room, failing conscious spatial recall tests.
Despite zero declarative memory of where rooms were located, Eugene stood up when hungry, walked straight to the kitchen cabinet, and retrieved snacks effortlessly.
On an eight-pair object-discrimination habit task, Eugene rose from roughly 50 percent chance to over 85 percent accuracy across 36 sessions without knowing how he chose.
Ann Graybiel's tetrode recordings in the dorsolateral striatum revealed 'task-bracketing' activity: sharp neural bursts at the start cue and final reward, with quiet firing in the middle.
Early in training, striatal neurons fire continuously throughout a T-maze run while dorsomedial striatum and prefrontal circuits evaluate choices.
Once a routine is overtrained into an automatic habit, activity shifts to the dorsolateral sensorimotor striatum and compresses into one chunked start-to-finish bracket.
In outcome-devaluation tests, animals with overtrained dorsolateral striatal brackets keep running toward a devalued food well even after losing appetite for the reward.
Kyle Smith and Ann Graybiel showed in 2013 that brief optogenetic inhibition of infralimbic cortex during run onset disrupts ingrained habits within seconds, unmasking older routines.
When the suppressed circuit is re-illuminated, the original chunked habit returns immediately, proving old habits remain latent rather than erased.

wow_facts.fact: Patient Eugene Pauly could navigate a 2-mile neighborhood walk and find his kitchen snacks while unable to sketch a single room of his house.
wow_facts.why_surprising: It proves complex daily navigation can run on pure striatal autopilot with zero conscious map.

wow_facts.fact: Once a habit is locked in, striatal neurons go nearly silent during the middle of the action and fire mainly at the very beginning and very end.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Your brain literally compresses a multi-step routine into a single 'open-and-close' file.

wow_facts.fact: Shutting down a tiny patch of cortex with light broke an entrenched habit in seconds — and a second flash brought the old habit right back.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Old habits are never deleted from the striatum; they are merely outcompeted.

wow_facts.fact: Eugene reached over 85 percent accuracy on a multi-object test while insisting every trial that he had never seen the objects in his life.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Skill and habit acquisition operate completely outside conscious awareness.

misconceptions.myth: Habits take exactly 21 days to form and willpower erases the neural trace.
misconceptions.truth: Habit consolidation varies widely by complexity, and striatal task-bracketing traces persist latently even after behavioral suppression.

misconceptions.myth: Amnesia wipes out all forms of learning and daily independence.
misconceptions.truth: Medial temporal damage destroys episodic recall while sparing basal ganglia procedural and habit circuits.

misconceptions.myth: Your prefrontal cortex supervises every step of a familiar morning routine.
misconceptions.truth: During chunked execution, prefrontal oversight drops while dorsolateral striatum and motor cortex run the sequence.
Striatal brackets package extended multi-action sequences gated by specific environmental cues.

everyday_hooks: Unlocking your phone and opening the same social app before you consciously remember picking the phone up.
Driving a familiar commute home and realizing at the driveway that you barely remember the last five intersections.
Reaching for the kitchen snack shelf at 10 p.m. when you are not even physically hungry because the evening cue fired your start burst.
Typing an old password automatically with your fingers even after consciously memorizing a new one.
